newsitem.title: USA: W. African, Latam crudes rain on U.S. Gulf Coast.
newsitem.headline: W. African, Latam crudes rain on U.S. Gulf Coast.

text.p: West African and Latin American crudes continued to rain on the U.S. Gulf Coast on Tuesday, although demand remained spotty amid poor margins and refinery turnarounds, traders said.
North Sea crudes were scarce, reflecting the narrow spread between benchmarks West Texas Intermediate/Cushing and North Sea Brent.
The transatlantic gap stood around $1.15-25 a barrel Tuesday afternoon, down 10-15 cents from Monday afternoon, discouraging buyers and sellers alike, traders said.
In contrast, West African barrels were plentiful, with Bonny Light and Qua Iboe assessed at the equivalent to Dated Brent plus $1.80-90 a barrel.
Still, refiners were showing a finicky appetite.
"Demand is not really strong, especially for distillate-rich grades like Forcados", one Texas trader said.
Latin American crudes were equally abundant. Traders noted that sour crudes out of Mexico and Venezuela remained especially prominent, with pricing becoming increasingly aggressive.
The mounting short-haul supply continued to pressure U.S. domestic sours, with West Texas Sour fetching a sharp discount of $2.80 a barrel to WTI/Cushing on Tuesday.
Elsewhere in the region, Chile's state-owned oil company Empresa Nacional del Petroleo (ENAP) is seeking to buy 960,000 barrels of crude oil for delivery April 24-28, trade sources said.
The tender will be awarded March 6.
In its last purchase tender, ENAP bought some 960,000 barrels of Nigerian Qua Iboe crude for delivery April 8-12.
Among Colombian grades, sweet Cusiana was still assessed around WTI minus 20 cents barrel. Nine cargoes are loading in April.
Trades were in disagreement as to whether two or three cargoes of Cano Limon crude remained in the March loading program.
